<reason>A very close, high-quality debate. CON built a genuinely strong counter-case around the "which layer" question and landed real hits: the strict-vs-toggle fork, the toll-collector reversal (developer takes 70%), the "500 purchases flow through one card" flip, and catching PRO's drift from calling adult ID a "strawman" to embracing verification-to-opt-out. But PRO's central route survived: default protections bind children before anyone identifies them, including the child on a parent's account or one who lied about age, whereas CON's fix (as CON conceded in B4.1) only defaults on for accounts already flagged as children's. CON's counter that "both models fail the account-sharing child identically" is overstated—it assumes the parent actively opts out, whereas CON's model leaves the parent's account unprotected by default. PRO also had an unanswered point that design-level features (odds disclosure, near-miss timers, laundered currencies) can only be addressed at the developer layer, and PRO's "if the economics collapse when kids are protected, they were predatory" framing went uncontested. CON's privacy cost is real but PRO's "verify once to remove protections" made it a bounded tradeoff. Both sides had one clipped turn. PRO wins narrowly because its protection advantage remains live while CON's "cost without protection" claim rests on an overstatement.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B2.2/B4.5 fork—forcing PRO to choose between toggles that aren't "strict" and identity checks for every adult, then showing PRO embraced the branch it had called a strawman—was the sharpest exchange, though PRO's A4.3–A4.4 answer (defaults bind everyone; only opt-out requires ID) kept its case coherent and preserved the "child nobody catches" advantage CON never fully neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
